entry.title: Bayesian MI-LASSO for Variable Selection on Multiply-Imputed Data

link.title: Bayesian MI-LASSO for Variable Selection on Multiply-Imputed Data

entry.content: Multiple imputation is widely used for handling missing data in real-world applications. For variable selection on multiply-imputed datasets, however, if selection is performed on each imputed dataset separately, it can result in different sets of selected variables across datasets. MI-LASSO, one of the most commonly used approaches to this problem, regards the same variable across all separate imputed datasets as a group variable and exploits the group LASSO to yield a consistent variable selection across all the multiply-imputed datasets. In this paper, we extend MI-LASSO into the Bayesian framework and propose four Bayesian MI-LASSO models for variable selection on multiply-imputed data, including three shrinkage prior-based and one Spike-and-Slab prior-based methods. To overcome the limitations of traditional, ad hoc threshold-based model selection, we develop a principled four-step projection predictive procedure that provides robust variable selection. This procedure also facilitates approximately calibrated post-selection inference and attains near-nominal coverage under a correct selection model. Simulation studies showed that the Bayesian MI-LASSO outperformed MI-LASSO and other alternative approaches, achieving higher specificity and lower mean squared error across a range of settings. We further demonstrated these methods via a case study using a multiply-imputed dataset from the University of Michigan Dioxin Exposure Study. The R package BMIselect is available on CRAN.

entry.title: Detection of evolutionary shifts in variance under an Ornsten-Uhlenbeck model

link.title: Detection of evolutionary shifts in variance under an Ornsten-Uhlenbeck model

entry.content: Sudden changes in environmental conditions can lead to evolutionary shifts not only in the optimal trait value (theta), but also in the diffusion variance (sigma^2) under the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model. While several methods have been developed to detect shifts in optimal values, few explicitly account for concurrent shifts in both evolutionary variance and diffusion variance. We use a multi-optima and multi-variance OU model to describe trait evolution with shifts in both theta and sigma^2, and analyze how covariance between species is affected when shifts in variance occur along the phylogeny. We propose a new method that simultaneously detects shifts in both variance and optimal values by formulating the problem as a variable selection task using an L1-penalized loss function. Our method is implemented in the R package ShiVa (Detection of evolutionary shifts in variance). Through simulations, we compare ShiVa with existing methods that can automatically detect evolutionary shifts under the OU model (l1ou, PhylogeneticEM, and PCMFit). Our method demonstrates improved predictive ability and significantly reduces false positives in detecting optimal value shifts when variance shifts are present. When only shifts in optimal value occur, our method performs comparably to existing approaches. We apply ShiVa to empirical data on floral diameter in Rafflesiaceae (with Euphorbiaceae outgroups) and buccal morphology in Centrarchidae sunfishes.

entry.title: Causal inference for N-of-1 trials

link.title: Causal inference for N-of-1 trials

entry.content: The aim of personalized medicine is to tailor treatment decisions to individuals’ characteristics. N-of-1 trials are within-person crossover trials that hold the promise of targeting individual-specific effects. While the idea behind N-of-1 trials might seem simple, analyzing and interpreting N-of-1 trials is not straightforward. Here we ground N-of-1 trials in a formal causal inference framework and formalize intuitive claims from the N-of-1 trials literature. We focus on causal inference from a single N-of-1 trial and define a conditional average treatment effect (CATE) that represents a target in this setting, which we call the U-CATE. We discuss assumptions sufficient for identification and estimation of the U-CATE under different causal models where the treatment schedule is assigned at baseline. A simple mean difference is an unbiased, asymptotically normal estimator of the U-CATE in simple settings. We also consider settings where carryover effects, trends over time, time-varying common causes of the outcome, and outcome-outcome effects are present. In these more complex settings, we show that a time-varying g-formula identifies the U-CATE under explicit assumptions. Finally, we analyze data from N-of-1 trials about acne symptoms and show how different assumptions about the data generating process can lead to different analytical strategies.

entry.title: Online conformal inference for multi-step time series forecasting

link.title: Online conformal inference for multi-step time series forecasting

entry.content: We study the construction of distribution-free prediction intervals for multi-step time series forecasting. In this setting, forecast errors at different horizons are serially dependent, and feedback is delayed, since the error of an h-step-ahead forecast becomes available only after h periods. We propose autocorrelated multi-step conformal prediction (AcMCP), an online procedure that accommodates delayed feedback and explicitly incorporates the dependence among multi-step forecast errors into conformal calibration. To characterize this dependence, we derive first-order representations of the optimal forecast errors under a general nonstationary autoregressive data-generating process, with explicit bounds on remainder terms. AcMCP guarantees long-run coverage of at least the nominal level at every horizon, without requiring exchangeability or any assumption on how the data distribution evolves over time. We also establish a finite-sample bound on the empirical coverage shortfall, which depends on the forecast horizon and the evaluation sample size. Notably, these guarantees do not rely on the accuracy of the linear approximations. Simulations and real-data applications show that AcMCP adapts to time-varying dynamics and maintains rolling coverage close to the nominal level. By exploiting the dependence among multi-step errors, it often yields narrower intervals than its counterpart without this dependence, with similar coverage, particularly at longer horizons.

entry.title: Likelihood-free Posterior Density Learning for Uncertainty Quantification in Inference Problems

link.title: Likelihood-free Posterior Density Learning for Uncertainty Quantification in Inference Problems

entry.content: Generative models and those with computationally intractable likelihoods are widely used to describe complex systems in the natural sciences, social sciences, and engineering. Fitting these models to data requires likelihood-free inference methods that explore the parameter space without explicit likelihood evaluations, relying instead on sequential simulation, which comes at the cost of computational efficiency and extensive tuning. We develop an alternative framework called kernel-adaptive synthetic posterior estimation (KASPE) that uses deep learning to directly reconstruct the mapping between the observed data and a finite-dimensional parametric representation of the posterior distribution, trained on a large number of simulated datasets. We provide theoretical justification for KASPE and a formal connection to the likelihood-based approach of expectation propagation. Simulation experiments demonstrate KASPE’s flexibility and performance relative to existing likelihood-free methods including approximate Bayesian computation in challenging inferential settings involving posteriors with heavy tails, multiple local modes, and over the parameters of a nonlinear dynamical system.

entry.title: Stochastic Derivative Estimation for Discontinuous Sample Performances: A Leibniz Integration Perspective

link.title: Stochastic Derivative Estimation for Discontinuous Sample Performances: A Leibniz Integration Perspective

entry.content: Based on the multidimensional Leibniz integral rule, we propose a novel unbiased stochastic derivative estimation framework for sample performance functions that are discontinuous in the parameter of interest. In this framework, for general discontinuities, a change of variables followed by the Leibniz integral rule generally yields a multi-run estimator, whereas for indicator-type discontinuities, a suitable transformation of the sample performance leads directly to a single-run estimator. The new framework includes existing likelihood ratio (LR)-based approaches as special cases and applies more broadly. In particular, it encompasses generalized LR (GLR) methods and the new formulation permits us to obtain much milder and simpler sufficient regularity conditions for these estimators to be unbiased, compared with the conditions given in previous papers. We also provide guidance on how to construct efficient single-run estimators in settings where existing methods may require the simulation of multiple sample paths or may be inapplicable. We validate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework through an inventory-price control problem.

entry.title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models

link.title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models

entry.content: Generalized linear models (GLMs) are fundamental tools for statistical modeling, with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) serving as the classical approach for parameter inference. While MLE performs well for canonical GLMs, it can become computationally challenging in more general settings with non-canonical, non-smooth, or saturating link functions, where the resulting optimization landscape may be ill-conditioned, non-convex, or non-differentiable. In this paper, we study an alternative estimation framework based on variational inequalities (VIs), which formulates GLM estimation through an operator-based equilibrium condition rather than likelihood minimization. We analyze the VI estimator from a statistical perspective and establish finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic normality, together with convergence guarantees for fixed-point and stochastic approximation algorithms. The framework accommodates a broad class of link functions, including non-canonical, non-smooth, and non-monotone cases satisfying a strong Minty-type condition, and extends naturally to generalized additive models (GAMs) via basis expansion. Numerical experiments demonstrate that under a fixed iteration budget, the VI approach achieves competitive estimation accuracy and faster, more stable convergence than MLE, particularly in GLMs and GAMs with non-canonical or non-smooth link functions.

entry.title: A Poisson Factor Mixture Model for the Analysis of Linguistic Competence

link.title: A Poisson Factor Mixture Model for the Analysis of Linguistic Competence

entry.content: Dependence among variables and unobserved heterogeneity are common features of multivariate count data. We propose a model-based clustering approach for this setting based on a Poisson factor mixture model, which combines a low-dimensional latent structure with a finite mixture specification. This enables simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering while providing interpretable latent representations of count profiles. The proposal originates from the UniversITA project, which collected formal written texts from a representative sample of Italian university students. Since university students play a central role in the process of linguistic change, as they are the most educated segment of the youth population, understanding variation in their writing is substantively important for both language research and higher education policy. Texts were annotated for various linguistic features, producing multivariate count data. The fitted model identifies two correlated latent dimensions of writing competence, interpretable as communicative effectiveness and grammatical-linguistic control. Incorporating educational and sociodemographic covariates further reveals distinct student profiles associated with field of study and prior educational background. Beyond this application, the proposed framework can be employed for the analysis of heterogeneous multivariate count data with complex dependence patterns, such as those arising in educational assessments, psychological and behavioral studies, and text analysis.

entry.title: Proxy-Reliance Control in Conformal Recalibration of One-Sided Value-at-Risk

link.title: Proxy-Reliance Control in Conformal Recalibration of One-Sided Value-at-Risk

entry.content: We introduce a proxy-reliance-controlled conformal recalibration framework for one-sided Value-at-Risk (VaR), and study a question that existing state-aware methods do not usually isolate: how strongly should the recalibration adjustment depend on an imperfect volatility proxy? We formalize this through a proxy-reliance parameter that continuously interpolates between an approximately constant-shift correction and a fully proxy-scaled correction. This makes proxy reliance a distinct and practically interpretable design choice in one-sided VaR recalibration. We show theoretically that larger proxy reliance increases the responsiveness of the tail adjustment to proxy scale, but also increases stressed-state fragility when the proxy underreacts. Empirically, in rolling out-of-sample tests on a six-ETF panel with VIX-linked state variables, and with supporting evidence from SPY, we find that the empirical value of proxy-reliance control lies in improved stressed-state robustness rather than uniform overall dominance. In particular, when the baseline forecast remains exposed to proxy imperfection in stressed states, lower or intermediate proxy reliance can outperform fully proxy-scaled recalibration in stressed left-tail VaR control.

entry.title: From multilayer networks to covariates: Layer-specific community detection

link.title: From multilayer networks to covariates: Layer-specific community detection

entry.content: We study layer-specific community detection in multilayer networks with heterogeneous community memberships and degree distributions. Membership mismatch complicates cross-layer information pooling, whereas sparsity heterogeneity can provide complementary signals for poorly connected communities. We recast the problem as network-with-covariates clustering: the target layer is retained as the primary network, while the remaining layers are converted into nodal covariates through our regularized spectral construction approach. We then perform community detection using a node-adaptive balancing scheme that relies more on the target network for high-degree nodes and more on the constructed covariates for low-degree nodes. Under a multilayer degree-corrected stochastic blockmodel, we establish guarantees for the constructed covariates and weak consistency when the average membership mismatch vanishes. Under additional degree structure and node-specific mismatch conditions, we establish strong consistency while allowing the average membership mismatch to remain nonvanishing. Simulations show that our proposed approach achieves the lowest misclustering error rates under most scenarios. An application to international food-trading networks reveals interpretable product-specific community structures.

entry.title: The Illusion of Learning from Observational Data: An Empirical Bayes Perspective

link.title: The Illusion of Learning from Observational Data: An Empirical Bayes Perspective

entry.content: Randomized experiments have long been the gold standard for scientists seeking to learn about cause and effect. When randomized experiments are infeasible, scientists often resort to observational studies, which are widely available and often large but rely on untestable assumptions that, when violated, may result in biased estimates. Uncertainty about bias leads to a phenomenon known as the illusion of learning from observational research (Gerber, Green and Kaplan, 2004a): absent prior information about bias, observational results cannot meaningfully contribute to the estimation of a causal parameter. To shatter the illusion, we take an empirical Bayes perspective. We show that the distribution of observational biases can be learned from calibration studies-experiments that target a causal effect that is known a priori to be zero. Calibration identifies the distribution of observational bias and allows observational studies to inform the estimation of causal parameters via empirical Bayes shrinkage. We formalize the illusion phenomenon in an empirical Bayes setting and show that, with an increasing number of calibration and observation studies, both the bias distribution and the causal effect can be consistently recovered. We illustrate our method through a simulation study and a semi-synthetic application based on Ferraro and Miranda (2013)’s water-usage experiment.

entry.title: Hyper Input Convex Neural Networks for Shape Constrained Learning and Optimal Transport

link.title: Hyper Input Convex Neural Networks for Shape Constrained Learning and Optimal Transport

entry.content: We introduce Hyper Input Convex Neural Networks (HyCNNs), a novel neural network architecture designed for learning convex functions. HyCNNs combine the principles of Maxout networks with input convex neural networks (ICNNs) to create a neural network that is always convex in the input, theoretically capable of leveraging depth, and performs reliably when trained at scale compared to ICNNs. Concretely, we prove that HyCNNs require exponentially fewer parameters than ICNNs to approximate quadratic functions up to a given precision. Throughout a series of synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that HyCNNs outperform existing ICNNs and MLPs in terms of predictive performance for convex regression and interpolation tasks. We further apply HyCNNs to learn high-dimensional optimal transport maps for synthetic examples and for single-cell data, where they oftentimes outperform ICNN-based neural optimal transport methods and other baselines across a wide range of setting.

entry.title: Improving Minority Population Sampling with BISG Probabilities: Evidence from a Survey of Jewish Americans

link.title: Improving Minority Population Sampling with BISG Probabilities: Evidence from a Survey of Jewish Americans

entry.content: Sampling geographically dispersed minority populations poses substantial challenges when individual group membership cannot be directly observed. Although stratified sampling can offer efficiency gains, these gains are typically modest unless the minority population is highly concentrated within a small number of strata. In this paper, we propose using Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) to enhance the efficiency of minority population sampling. BISG generates individual-level probabilities of minority group membership based on names and residential addresses. We incorporate these probabilities into a stratified Poisson probability sampling design. Applying the proposed approach to a national survey of Jewish Americans, we find that our estimates closely align with those from a large-scale Pew Research Center survey of the same population, which relied on a substantially more expensive sampling strategy involving geographic stratification and screening. At a fraction of the cost, our survey reproduces nearly identical patterns observed by Pew, including estimates of religious denomination prevalence and participation in specific religious activities.

entry.title: Empirical Bayes Rebiasing

link.title: Empirical Bayes Rebiasing

entry.content: We study methods for simultaneous analysis of many noisy and biased estimates, each paired with an even noisier estimate of its own bias. The analyst’s goal is to construct short calibrated intervals for each parameter. The standard debiasing approach, which subtracts the bias estimate from each biased estimate, inflates variance and yields long intervals. In this paper, we propose an empirical Bayes rebiasing strategy that starts from the fully debiased estimates and learns from data how much bias to reintroduce by estimating the unknown bias distribution. We provide convergence rates for the coverage of our intervals when the bias distribution is estimated using nonparametric maximum likelihood. Furthermore, we demonstrate substantial precision gains in prediction-powered inference, including pairwise LLM win-rate evaluations, as well as for inference of direct genetic effects in family-based GWAS.

entry.title: An Energy-Driven Framework for Privacy-Aware Synthetic Data Generation

link.title: An Energy-Driven Framework for Privacy-Aware Synthetic Data Generation

entry.content: Access to microdata in official statistics requires balancing disclosure risk and statistical utility. This paper proposes an interpretable, open-box energy-driven framework for privacy-aware synthesis of mixed-type tabular data, combining discriminative modelling, Bayesian-network proposals, Metropolis–Hastings sampling and post-generation optimization. Explicit energy components govern record-level plausibility, proximity to training records and diversity, while target selection balances fidelity and classification utility, making these trade-offs directly inspectable. Evaluation uses an artificially constructed individual-level dataset with demographic, behavioural and health-related variables. entry.title: U-centering as subset ANOVA: edge regression and higher-order theory

link.title: U-centering as subset ANOVA: edge regression and higher-order theory

entry.content: Unbiased squared distance covariance and the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC) are fourth-order U-statistics, yet U-centering evaluates them from pairwise arrays in $O(n^2)$ operations. We show that U-centering is exactly least-squares residualization after fitting additive endpoint effects. This analysis of variance (ANOVA) interpretation explains the zero row sums and the normalization through residual degrees of freedom. The same geometry gives regression representations of dependence and two-sample statistics, exact permutation variances, and relations among pooled and regression mean squares. For arrays indexed by $r$-element subsets and $n\ge2r$, higher-order U-centering removes all lower-order subset effects and projects onto a space of dimension $\binom{n}{r}-\binom{n}{r-1}$. For fixed symmetric square-integrable kernels evaluated on independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) paired observations, we derive the residual covariance matrix, exact mean-squared errors for estimating the highest-order Hoeffding components, unbiased positive semidefinite (PSD) covariance estimates, and moment formulas under independence and permutation. The normalized residual inner product equals a direct unbiased estimator involving up to $2r$ observations, but can be evaluated in $O(n^r)$ operations for fixed $r$. For four-argument matching kernels, three matrix products yield exactly unbiased estimators of a fourth spectral moment of kernel cross-covariance in $O(n^3)$ arithmetic and $O(n^2)$ storage. A numerical illustration distinguishes dependence structures with equal HSIC and different spectral concentration.

entry.title: The Earth Moves, But So Does the Bias: Systematic Upward Bias of the Wasserstein (Earth Mover’s) Distance and Permutation-Based Null Calibration

link.title: The Earth Moves, But So Does the Bias: Systematic Upward Bias of the Wasserstein (Earth Mover’s) Distance and Permutation-Based Null Calibration

entry.content: The Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) is gaining increasing interest among political scientists for assessing similarity in preference distributions. Existing applications predominantly involve relatively large samples and low-dimensional response spaces, which can mitigate finite-sample distortions. However, empirical EMD remains biased upward due to sampling variation in empirical probability measures. This problem is often overlooked and becomes especially severe in high-dimensional or sparse settings, including conjoint distributions that serve as an illustrative example in this paper. As political scientists are broadening their use cases of EMD, this paper cautions against interpreting standard bootstrap uncertainty bounds as a correction for the upward bias of empirical EMD. It proposes a permutation-based null calibration framework for more robust hypothesis testing. As a non-parametric approach, it frees researchers from making directional or distributional shape assumptions. While alternative estimators require these rigid assumptions to correct for upward bias, political science data often fail to meet them in practice. Through four sets of Monte Carlo simulations, this paper demonstrates the utility of this framework. The proposed approach also applies more generally to empirical comparisons of two probability distributions defined on a common metric space, provided that the ground distance between support points is substantively meaningful.

entry.title: Estimating Treatment Effects Through Intermediate-Event Pathways with Multi-State Data

link.title: Estimating Treatment Effects Through Intermediate-Event Pathways with Multi-State Data

entry.content: During clinical trials evaluating a drug’s effect on a survival endpoint, intermediate events often occur before the primary event. The treatment can affect the primary event through multiple pathways via intermediate events. With multiple intermediate events, each is a treatment-induced confounder of transitions out of the others, so we cannot identify natural or separable effects. We instead consider stochastic interventions that assign each transition the identifiable observed-history hazard of either arm. Contrasts between the resulting counterfactual cumulative incidences define transition-, event-, and path-targeted effects, identifiable without cross-world or isolation assumptions. Based on the efficient influence functions for the counterfactual cumulative incidences under hypothetical interventions, we construct multiply robust and semiparametrically efficient estimators for these targeted treatment effects. Our proposed framework quantifies treatment effects through each transition, on each event, and along each path. By analyzing data from the LEADER trial, we find that liraglutide significantly reduces the risk of cardiovascular and microvascular events. The reduction in all-cause mortality is primarily mediated by its effects on expanded major adverse cardiovascular events.

entry.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

link.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

entry.content: Semicontinuous outcomes characterized by an exact zero mass and heavy-tailed continuous distributions challenge empirical risk modeling and machine learning. Compound Poisson-Gamma Tweedie processes impose a rigid mean-variance coupling that distorts zero-mass probabilities under extreme tail dispersion, flattening continuous density and reducing extreme-risk discrimination. Furthermore, heuristic post-hoc target capping introduces systematic bias while leaving loss gradients vulnerable to tail leverage. We present a unified, statistically coherent likelihood framework for semicontinuous modeling under arbitrary zero-inflation and explicit upper boundary constraints. Optimization and likelihood evaluations operate strictly in a latent space defined by the power-scaling mapping $y_i^* = \min{(y_i/s)^\lambda, U^*}$, where $s \in (0, U)$ anchors scale and $\lambda \in (0,1)$ regularizes tail curvature. The architecture partitions the response into three regimes: an unconstrained Bernoulli hurdle, an analytical continuous Gamma body, and an upper boundary point mass governed by incomplete Gamma survival ratios. Rather than an arbitrary truncation, the boundary functions as an intrinsic tail accumulator bounding score and Hessian dynamics. We derive the closed-form deviance objective, score vectors, and block-diagonal Hessian matrix, proving that parameter spaces are information-orthogonal to enable concurrent classification and regression updates. Asymptotic boundary analysis demonstrates that score and curvature scale linearly in the deep tail, establishing a quadratic restoring force that prevents gradient collapse. The framework breaks the Tweedie parameter rigidity paradox while maintaining structural fidelity across both zero occurrence and extreme severity differentiation.

entry.title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on “Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments”

link.title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on “Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments”

entry.content: We comment on the optimally-transported generalized method of moments (OTGMM) of Schennach and Starck (2026) and give counterexamples to Theorems 2-6. In the small-error analysis, the assumptions do not ensure consistency or asymptotic normality (Theorems 2-3). In the large-error analysis, Theorem 4 states the equivalence between the OTGMM estimator and the GMM estimator with modified moments, and Theorems 5-6 assert consistency and asymptotic normality. Through counterexamples, we show that the equivalence in Theorem 4 fails and a component of the Lagrange multiplier has different limits under the two estimators (Theorems 5-6). We also point out that, under misspecification, the population value selected by OTGMM depends on the metric. We give sufficient conditions and establish results following the original motivation for OTGMM. Our corrections to Theorems 4-6 change their assumptions or interpretation more substantially than those to Theorems 2 and 3. Furthermore, we correct Assumption 16 and the test’s null distribution.

entry.title: High-dimensional Gaussian Graphical Model Testing for Long-Memory Time Series

link.title: High-dimensional Gaussian Graphical Model Testing for Long-Memory Time Series

entry.content: Many real-world high-dimensional time series exhibit long-memory, but Gaussian graphical model testing in this regime remains understudied. We develop a direct, data-adaptive test statistic for assessing conditional independence in the graph structure of stationary Gaussian time series. We establish a finite-sample, Berry–Esseen type Gaussian approximation bound for the statistic, which applies to both short-memory and long-memory time series. The testing procedure uses a block bootstrap method, on which we provide a finite-sample validity result including in the ultra-high-dimensional scenario, and can be extended to comparing graphical structures in two-sample tests. We also develop a consistency-empowered correction to the statistic and show that such tests attain asymptotic consistency in both size and power. Our proposed method is applied to real-world fMRI data to understand functional connectivities within brain in different periods.

entry.title: Quantifying Inconsistent Mediation: The Mediated Magnitude Share and the Degree of Suppression

link.title: Quantifying Inconsistent Mediation: The Mediated Magnitude Share and the Degree of Suppression

entry.content: The proportion mediated (PM), the indirect effect divided by the total effect, is intuitive when direct and indirect effects act in the same direction. Under inconsistent mediation, however, opposing pathways partially cancel, so PM can fall outside the unit interval and becomes unstable as the total effect approaches zero. We propose two complementary effect-scale measures: the mediated magnitude share (MMS), which quantifies the absolute magnitude of an indirect pathway relative to the combined absolute magnitudes of the direct and indirect pathways, and the degree of suppression, which quantifies the fraction of this combined magnitude cancelled by opposing pathways. Both measures are bounded between 0 and 1, and MMS reduces to PM under consistent mediation. We extend both measures to multiple indirect pathways and, through a logarithmic transformation, to binary outcomes on ratio scales. In simulations with continuous and binary outcomes, PM estimates were highly dispersed when the total effect was small relative to the pathway magnitudes, whereas estimates of MMS and the degree of suppression remained bounded. We illustrate the measures using previously published estimates from the Adolescents Training and Learning to Avoid Steroids (ATLAS) program, where PM was $-0.30$, MMS was $0.19$, and the degree of suppression was $0.38$, showing how the two measures describe the relative pathway magnitudes and their cancellation under inconsistent mediation.

entry.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series

link.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series

entry.content: The logarithmic vector multiplicative error model (log-vMEM) provides a methodology for modeling and forecasting multivariate positive-valued time series. However, the number of autoregressive parameters increases rapidly with the system dimension and lag order, posing challenges for estimation and model selection. This paper develops a regularized estimation framework for the log-vMEM with multivariate Gamma errors by incorporating hierarchical lag structures to induce sparsity and accommodate heterogeneous lag dynamics. We consider three hierarchical lag structures: componentwise, own-other, and elementwise, in combination with group lasso, group MCP, and group SCAD, adaptive group lasso penalties. Parameter estimation is carried out through an alternating block-coordinate optimization algorithm with sequential Gauss-Seidel updates, while GPU-accelerated numerical quadrature is employed to address the computational burden of evaluating the multivariate Gamma likelihood. Simulation experiments investigate parameter recovery and lag selection under different sparsity structures. The real data analysis is carried out on the realized volatility measures for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) which allows a comparison of the competing regularization approaches in an empirical financial setting. Together, these developments provide a computational framework for sparse multivariate volatility modeling with flexible lag structures and dependent Gamma errors.

entry.title: When Statisticians Can Also Be AI Engineers, What Could We Build?

link.title: When Statisticians Can Also Be AI Engineers, What Could We Build?

entry.content: Statistical software makes methods widely available. Good statistical work, however, requires understanding the question, how the data were collected, and what conclusions the evidence can support. As AI agents make data analysis accessible to people without statistical training, this reasoning should be built into the systems themselves. Our review of selected AI agents for data analysis and study design points to a gap in documented support for scientific inquiry with users at runtime. In this paper, we advocate designing domain-specific interactive harnesses in which statistical principles guide proactive inquiry: agents recognize missing information that could change an analysis, ask questions users may not know to raise, and use the answers to guide or revise analytical decisions. Two practical entry points illustrate how statisticians can begin building: an implemented causal-consulting skill within an existing agent environment and Model Forge, a custom harness for interactive model and algorithm development. These design examples connect statistical principles to choices about context, memory, tools, and interfaces, and motivate evaluation of both computational correctness and the scientific consequences of interaction. We conclude with a broader interdisciplinary research agenda on adaptive human-agent interaction, including selective information acquisition, evolving user preferences, and evaluation under uncertainty.

entry.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis

link.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis

entry.content: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56{,}202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2{,}000 reports, the chains recover 90.8\% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1{,}205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.

entry.title: dsp: An R Package for Bayesian Time Series Modeling with the Dynamic Shrinkage Process

link.title: dsp: An R Package for Bayesian Time Series Modeling with the Dynamic Shrinkage Process

entry.content: dsp provides a unified state-space framework for modeling nonstationary time series using the Dynamic Shrinkage Process (DSP), a class of global-local shrinkage priors. DSP adaptively regularizes time-varying parameters to shrink noise while preserving abrupt changes and other local structure. The package supports Gaussian and count-data smoothing, changepoint detection, time-varying parameter regression, and volatility estimation, with posterior predictive draws available for missing-value imputation and forecasting. Nonstationary time series often contain periods of relative stability punctuated by abrupt changes in mean or variance. dsp offers a common interface for model specification, posterior computation, summarization, and visualization across models that were previously developed separately in the literature. Core functionality is implemented in C++ via Rcpp for computational efficiency. We describe the underlying models, package design, and the main functions for fitting, summarizing, and plotting posterior results.

entry.title: Sample size calculation comparing two survival curves in the presence of nonproportional hazards utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time using two different Weibull distributions

link.title: Sample size calculation comparing two survival curves in the presence of nonproportional hazards utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time using two different Weibull distributions

entry.content: Sample size calculations in two-arm clinical trials with survival endpoint often utilize the proportional hazards (PH) assumption. In case of nonproportional hazards (NPH), much research is ongoing with some newer methods developed that work well in specific scenarios. Recent developments have considered the nonparametric Max-Combo logrank test for both design and analysis of survival data with NPH. Although many approaches have been proposed for analyzing time-to-event data with NPH such as Restricted Mean Survival Time, Average Hazard Ratios, and piecewise exponential model with hazard ratios changing over time, translation into sample size calculation is not obvious and relies on simulations for very specific scenarios of NPH. In the parametric setting, accelerated failure time models that allow NPH but require a constant time ratio assumption (PT assumption) have been proposed. Recently, a parametric approach that simultaneously allows both nonproportional hazards (NPH) and nonproportional time (NPT) has been proposed. It utilizes the concept of Relative Time (RT) with two different Weibull distributions for the two trial arms in the case of monotonically increasing/decreasing time ratios. A key limitation is that the hypotheses leading to the sample size calculation rely on a single effect size defined at a specific survival percentile. In our current work, we extend the parent RT method by utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time (WRT) that allows us comparison of the full survival curves. Performance of the proposed method is compared to the Max-Combo method under different weighting schemes, and its operation characteristics are studied via simulations.

entry.content: We develop specification tests for parametric conditional tail index models of heavy-tailed distributions. The rule allows lower thresholds to retain more observations for testing while limiting size distortions, with potential gains in power. The finite sample performance of the tests is examined through simulations and a real data application.

link.title: Clouded Representatives and Score Matching for Distributed Quantile Regression

entry.content: Quantile regression is widely used in high-stakes applications where the data are distributed across many sites and the individual records cannot be shared. The existing distributed methods for quantile regression typically require homogeneous sites, large sites, or synchronous communication, which are rarely all satisfied in practice. In this paper, we propose a new method named cloudqr. Each site summarizes its observations by a few Gaussian clouds, each given by the size, center, and covariance of a group of observations, such that the clouds match the score of the raw data exactly. A central server then fits the quantile regression on the clouds from all sites. We establish the convergence of cloudqr under mild conditions. entry.title: When Do Sports Leagues Stop Being Competitive? Bayesian Detection of Competitive-Balance Eras from Match-Level Data

link.title: When Do Sports Leagues Stop Being Competitive? Bayesian Detection of Competitive-Balance Eras from Match-Level Data

entry.content: Competitive balance shapes outcome uncertainty, fan interest, and league regulation, yet standard measures summarize realized standings and cannot separate structural ability differences from match-level randomness. We develop a Bayesian framework that infers structural competitive balance from longitudinal match outcomes. Team abilities are obtained by projecting Gaussian auxiliary variables onto a graph-fused l1 polytope whose radius measures total pairwise ability variation. The projection places positive probability on exact ties, so statistically indistinguishable teams form explicit rank tiers. The radius equals realized ability variation whenever the constraint binds, linking it to parity, detectability, and structural inequality. An adaptive finite-regime model lets competitive eras recur, emerge, and disappear while team hierarchies remain season specific. Simulations show accurate recovery of regimes, radii, abilities, and tiers. Applied to 25 English Premier League seasons, the model identifies a persistent shift to a more stratified league beginning in 2005/06, with 2010/11 the only later return to the compressed regime. It also shows that a close title race can coexist with wide league-wide separation and that head-to-head results can separate clubs level on points. The framework gives leagues a model-based measure of balance to inform debates on revenue sharing and financial regulation.

entry.title: Adversarial Multiplicity: Cherry-Picked Models and the Limits of Disclosure

link.title: Adversarial Multiplicity: Cherry-Picked Models and the Limits of Disclosure

entry.content: Predictive multiplicity – where similarly accurate models disagree on individual predictions – can be leveraged to optimize secondary metrics (e.g., fairness) without loss in predictive performance. However, exploiting multiplicity opens the opportunity for motivated parties (or coding agents gaming their objectives) to steer predictions toward their own ends, such as in litigation or consumer disputes with automated decision-making tools. In these adversarial multiplicity settings, we distinguish soft manipulation, where parties optimize over innocuous model choices (e.g., hyperparameter tuning, feature engineering), from hard manipulation, where parties directly perturb model parameters. We find a sufficiently flexible model can be manipulated to reverse any individual prediction with minimal change in predictive performance while passing black-box audits, making hard manipulation viable in most regulatory settings. Soft manipulation has smaller effects but can pass white-box audits requiring full access to code and data. Even aggregate estimates can be manipulated: a model’s estimated effect of climate change on wildfires can be fully reversed by hard edits and soft search. We find the Reconcile algorithm typically resolves most disagreements between models, but more often in favor of the manipulator when the opposing model is chosen adversarially compared to at random. We map which manipulations can plausibly pass existing regulations and disclosure policies, and recommend mitigations such as pre-registration, proof of model training, sensitivity analyses, multi-metric evaluations, and committing to versioned public models.

entry.title: A Unified Coordinate Descent Framework for Penalized Longitudinal Log-Contrast Quantile Regression

link.title: A Unified Coordinate Descent Framework for Penalized Longitudinal Log-Contrast Quantile Regression

entry.content: Quantile regression characterizes heterogeneous covariate effects across the response distribution, but its extension to high-dimensional longitudinal compositional data poses substantial challenges, such as the nonsmooth check loss, the unit-sum structure of compositional covariates. Existing work is confined to Lasso penalization, and does not readily extend to nonconvex penalties. We propose CDaLCqr, a unified coordinate descent algorithm for penalized longitudinal log-contrast quantile regression accommodating popular penalties, such as adaptive Lasso, smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD), and minimax concave penalty (MCP) within a single framework. The proposed method uses a Huber-type smooth approximation of the check loss and enforces the zero-sum constraint through an augmented Lagrangian formulation. CDaLCqr combines coordinate descent with majorization-minimization, yielding explicit updates through coordinate-wise quadratic surrogates. We show that the stopping tolerance controls errors in the zero-sum constraint and stationarity conditions. Under suitable conditions and sufficiently close initialization, we also prove local convergence of the coefficient and multiplier iterates, with an error bound decreasing by a fixed factor less than one each iteration. Simulations highlight the estimation advantages of SCAD and MCP variants and their sparse model identification. An application to Chinese provincial industrial data identifies interpretable, quantile-specific associations between sectoral composition and regional economic output.

entry.title: Changepoint localization via nested exchangeability tests: from point estimates to confidence intervals

link.title: Changepoint localization via nested exchangeability tests: from point estimates to confidence intervals

entry.content: We study distribution-free uncertainty quantification for a changepoint estimate in an offline setting. We observe a sequence with a single changepoint and are given an estimate of its location. The pre- and post-change segments are independent and each consists of i.i.d. (or, more generally, exchangeable) observations from arbitrary and unknown distributions. We introduce Changepoint LOcalization via Nested Exchangeability testing (CLONE), a novel method for constructing distribution-free confidence intervals around that estimate by testing exchangeability in nested windows centered at the reference estimate. Under these assumptions, CLONE provides finite-sample coverage for any black-box reference estimator. Using a geometrically shrinking radius grid, CLONE requires only $O(log n)$ permutation tests. We characterize optimal scores for the framework and provide practical recommendations that result in sharp confidence intervals. Under mild assumptions, CLONE confidence intervals have asymptotically vanishing normalized length. Simulations and experiments on image and text data support our theoretical findings.

entry.title: Inference after selection on randomized p-values

link.title: Inference after selection on randomized p-values

entry.content: We consider inference on parameters and hypotheses selected using p-values. We provide a simple procedure to decompose a p-value into two components, one for inference and one for selection, that are independent under the null hypothesis. To control the Type 1 error rate conditional on selection of the null hypothesis from randomized p-values, we develop tests motivated by the selective inference approaches of data thinning, fission, and carving. Unlike the typical application of these approaches, however, our tests only make use of the p-values rather than the full data. Furthermore, we construct confidence intervals that attain the nominal conditional coverage and corresponding estimators. In the context of the file drawer problem, the winner’s curse, and sequential testing, we show that our proposals offer both theoretical and empirical advantages over existing randomized and non-randomized approaches. Lastly, we apply our methods for selective inference on genetic associations using publicly-available p-values from the UK Biobank.

entry.title: Statistical and Privacy Guarantees for Deep M-Regression via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics

link.title: Statistical and Privacy Guarantees for Deep M-Regression via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics

entry.content: In this article, we study deep nonparametric regression trained via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD), a variant of stochastic gradient descent that injects carefully calibrated Gaussian noise during optimization. Using a PAC-Bayesian analysis tailored to deep ReLU networks, we establish an excess-risk bound that simultaneously accounts for network approximation error, statistical complexity, and the algorithmic cost accumulated along the SGLD trajectory. Under a Bernstein condition and within a stable SGLD regime, the excess-risk bound contains a stochastic term whose coefficient is inversely proportional to the variance of injected noise, while the estimator retains the optimal rate for nonparametric regression under the H"older smoothness condition up to logarithmic factors. This result provides an approximation-error-aware, rate-optimal statistical perspective on the widely observed generalization benefits of moderate SGLD noise. For per-sample clipped SGLD, we further establish an exact f-DP guarantee and the corresponding asymptotic $\mu$-GDP guarantee for the proposed estimator. We establish statistical convergence rates and differential privacy guarantees for DNN estimators trained using SGLD, while explicitly accounting for both network approximation error and the effect of injected noise in the excess-risk bound. Extensive simulation studies and analyses of two real datasets examine the finite-sample predictive performance and privacy-utility behavior of the proposed procedure.

entry.title: marp: Model-Averaged Inference for Parametric Renewal Processes in R

link.title: marp: Model-Averaged Inference for Parametric Renewal Processes in R

entry.content: Renewal processes model inter-event times between recurrent events using a parametric distribution, but selecting a single model can ignore model uncertainty and affect inference, particularly in small samples. This paper introduces marp, an R package for model-averaged inference in parametric renewal processes. The package fits six commonly used distributions, compares them using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, and reports selected-model and model-averaged estimates of the mean inter-event time, event probability and hazard function, with percentile and Studentised bootstrap confidence intervals. A simulation study under three data-generating models showed that model averaging did not improve point estimation but often improved interval coverage relative to the AIC-selected model. Applications to seizure-recurrence and engineering failure-time data illustrate the proposed methods. The marp package provides a reproducible framework for inference that accounts for model uncertainty in parametric renewal processes.

entry.title: Adaptive Experimentation Can Hide Model Error:Detection Limits and Falsification Budget

link.title: Adaptive Experimentation Can Hide Model Error:Detection Limits and Falsification Budget

entry.content: An experiment can be informative about the parameters of a working model and uninformative about whether that model is wrong. Adaptive design can reinforce this mismatch by repeatedly selecting settings where an incorrect model fits. We bound the power of any valid adequacy test in terms of the experimenter’s own sampling distribution, then distinguish information absent from the selected data from information lost by the detector. A computable diagnostic measures unresolved error relative to a declared expansion of the working model. It motivates a training-free rule that reserves part of the design budget for falsification. The empirical record is mixed: the independently specified primary study fails detection eligibility, and a later numerator diagnostic fails its improvement criteria. After the frozen rule fails on fresh continuous-null panels, a disclosed secondary horizon-calibrated revision detects 35.8% of misspecified campaigns versus 31.7% for a class-separation control at T = 240, but has no resolved advantage at T = 480. In a corrected 289-unit measured replay it improves on random design and trails class-discrimination EIG. A conditional futility bound explains why remaining time matters without proving the gate constant or its power. These results support separating parameter learning, model checking and detector performance; they do not establish a universally superior design policy or prospective scientific discovery.

entry.title: Identification and Bounding of Joint Expectation over Potential Outcomes

link.title: Identification and Bounding of Joint Expectation over Potential Outcomes

entry.content: The joint expectation of functions of potential outcomes $(Y_1,Y_0)$ is a fundamental quantity in causal inference, particularly when investigating the variation or heterogeneity of causal effects. This paper provides novel assumptions for their identification: comonotonicity and countercomonotonicity. These assumptions offer a unified framework for their identification across discrete, continuous, and mixed outcome variables. In the absence of these assumptions, we derive sharp bounds for two broad classes of functions, yielding new results for bounding moments of individual causal effects, which are central to measuring effect heterogeneity. We present corresponding estimation methods and illustrate them in simulation studies and real-world datasets.

entry.title: Bayesian Spatio-temporal Modeling of Multi-Site Wastewater Surveillance Data

link.title: Bayesian Spatio-temporal Modeling of Multi-Site Wastewater Surveillance Data

entry.content: Wastewater surveillance provides population-level evidence of infectious disease activity. As surveillance expands across multiple sites, repeated measurements must be analyzed jointly while accounting for differences among sites and the public health regions they represent. We develop a Bayesian spatio-temporal framework that decomposes wastewater measurements into a shared epidemic curve, spatially correlated regional deviations, persistent site effects, and within-site temporal dependence. This hierarchical decomposition accommodates unequal observation windows and sampling schedules, allowing regional trajectories to be compared while preserving site-level heterogeneity. A direct marginal spatial covariance specification further separates the magnitude of regional variation from the strength of association between neighboring regions, providing distinct interpretations of these two sources of spatial variation. We also introduce region-specific time shifts to distinguish regional leads and lags in epidemic timing from differences in signal levels and local fluctuations. Simulation studies demonstrate the recovery of these components and show that omitting true time shifts can lead to increased estimates of residual temporal variation. Application to Ontario SARS-CoV-2 wastewater surveillance data reveals persistent site heterogeneity, within-site temporal dependence, and spatial association among neighboring regions. Regional timing differences are more pronounced during the first year of Omicron than in the XBB-and-later period.

entry.title: Stay, Reposition, or Recharge: Battery-Aware Operation of Robotaxi Fleets

link.title: Stay, Reposition, or Recharge: Battery-Aware Operation of Robotaxi Fleets

entry.content: Electric robotaxis are rapidly expanding from pilots to scaled commercial deployment; unlike traditional human-driven ride-hailing vehicles, they require centralized fleet control and careful management of vehicle state of charge (SoC). We study how a fleet manager should jointly make service, empty repositioning, idling, and charging decisions in such systems. We develop a continuous-time fluid model in which vehicles evolve across location-charge states, and identify two forms of charge-aware control that are absent from classic repositioning models: early return-to-depot (RTD) and charge-aware repositioning. In particular, the optimal solution admits simple threshold structures. Each location has a battery threshold such that vehicles should return to the depot to recharge when their SoC is below it and should not do so when their SoC is above it. Vehicles should not reposition below the same threshold either; above it, the choice of destination depends on whether a vehicle’s SoC matches the destination’s battery sensitivity, a notion we introduce in the paper. We then quantify the value of charge awareness by comparing fully charge-aware policies with charge-oblivious policies that ignore SoC in RTD and repositioning decisions. We show that the performance gap can be unbounded, driven by a dilemma between under-utilizing high-charge vehicles and over-sending low-charge vehicles to locations from which charging is costly. A numerical case study calibrated using 2025 NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission trip records illustrates these thresholds and shows that charge-aware control can generate substantial gains in a realistic urban network. Importantly, simple threshold-based heuristics recover most of the value of the fully charge-aware solution.

link.title: Unobserved Consideration and Consumer Welfare

entry.content: Can welfare effects of price change be identified when consumers’ consideration sets are heterogeneous and unobserved? We establish that the welfare distribution is the same functional of structural choice probabilities under stable but limited consideration as under full consideration. The result permits unrestricted income-effects, preference heterogeneity, and dependence between preferences and consideration. Within this class, limited consideration admits a full-consideration representation preserving choice-probabilities and money-metric compensation: consideration/preferences can remain unidentified while demand and welfare are identified. When consideration sets contract as prices rise, the welfare distribution can be bounded using demand and a bound on choice-set attrition.

entry.title: Geometric Functional Inequalities for Markov Processes: An Invitation via the Langevin Diffusion

link.title: Geometric Functional Inequalities for Markov Processes: An Invitation via the Langevin Diffusion

entry.content: Functional inequalities provide a language for reasoning about the long-time properties of ergodic Markov processes in terms of their macroscopic geometry. This article offers an informal introduction to functional inequalities for readers who are more familiar with probabilistic tools based around couplings, Lyapunov techniques, and similar. The main ideas are developed through the overdamped Langevin diffusion, where various functionals related to this convergence admit particularly transparent expressions, and for which the key associated inequalities – namely, the Poincar'{e} and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities – are especially well-studied. We explain the qualitative content of these inequalities, what they imply about convergence to equilibrium, how they transform and compose under natural operations, and how they interface with classical probabilistic approaches. Related inequalities are discussed more briefly, and an annotated guide is provided for readers wishing to enter the wider literature.

entry.title: MSR-CP: A Modified Segmented Regression Approach to Change Point Estimation in Rainfall Patterns in West Bengal

link.title: MSR-CP: A Modified Segmented Regression Approach to Change Point Estimation in Rainfall Patterns in West Bengal

entry.content: This study presents a methodology for detecting change point in precipitation series using a smooth version of segmented regression model. We examine several existing change point detection methods and identify their limitations in capturing gradual changes commonly observed in climate data. To address these limitations, we discuss an extension of the traditional segmented regression model enabling the detection of gradual shifts in trend. The developed methodology is further extended to accommodate dependent error structures, which are common in time series data. Extensive simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the performance and computational efficiency of the proposed approach relative to existing methods. The methodology is subsequently applied to 60 years of monsoon rainfall data from two districts of West Bengal, India. This approach offers improved insights into evolving rainfall patterns and serves as a useful tool for climate data analysis and long-term forecasting.

entry.title: CountScan: Simultaneous Lower Bounds on Historical Watermark Matches over All Text Intervals

link.title: CountScan: Simultaneous Lower Bounds on Historical Watermark Matches over All Text Intervals

entry.content: A provider holding a watermark key may audit an external document and choose passages after reading it. A bound computed for a fixed passage is not valid for a passage chosen after seeing the evidence. One remedy splits the evidence between selection and validation. We take the other route and make the statement hold for every interval at once. CountScan gives finite-sample lower bounds on the number of retained historical watermark matches, simultaneously over all text intervals and count thresholds. Its validity rests on one condition: given the auditor’s information, the pivots of positions that are not history matches are conditionally super-uniform. This condition holds when generation uses the key only through the Gumbel-max rule and editors have no access to the key, so the guarantee covers edits that depend on the generated text when the calibrators are nonincreasing. Simultaneity raises the threshold by the logarithm of the document length; for a long interval this costs about that logarithm divided by the critical evidence value, in certified tokens. We give a finite-length expansion of the certified proportion, finite-sample rates for two-level rules with lower bounds of the same order within a pivot-only class, and an upper bound over a calibrator class. On pre-registered holdouts with OPT and Qwen base models at temperature one, CountScan certifies substantial counts; under heavy random edits it remains valid but loses most of its power.

entry.title: Generalized confidence intervals for the covariate-specific overlap coefficient

link.title: Generalized confidence intervals for the covariate-specific overlap coefficient

entry.content: Continuous diagnostic tests are often used to discriminate between diseased and healthy populations. Therefore, it is important to look for measures to assess the effectiveness of diagnostic markers in discriminating between these two states. The overlap coefficient (OVL), which is defined as the area of intersection of the graphs of two probability density functions, is considered as a summary measure of diagnostic accuracy. Often additional information is available on some of the covariates which are known to influence the accuracy of such measures. Consequently, in this work we incorporate covariate information using linear regression models with normally distributed errors, enabling the construction of the OVL estimator based on the ordinary least squares estimates of the regression coefficients. We further develop a method for constructing generalized confidence intervals for the covariate-specific overlap coefficient. A simulation study is conducted to assess the finite-sample performance of the proposed generalized confidence interval method and to compare it with other procedures. Finally, an illustration to assess the age-specific accuracy of glucose as a biomarker of diabetes is provided.

entry.title: Efficiently Estimating Cycle Statistics on Graphs via Spanning Trees

link.title: Efficiently Estimating Cycle Statistics on Graphs via Spanning Trees

entry.content: Simple cycles encode feedback and alternative routes in networks and are important for routing problems, the convergence of dynamical processes on networks, message passing and belief propagation, or even static network characterizations such as structural balance in signed networks. Being able to assess and sample from the cycle structure of a graph is thus of interest in many analysis contexts. However, due to the combinatorial growth of the cycle space with graph size, the computational cost for such sampling is high. Therefore, we here introduce a sampling framework that enables us to sample from the cycle structure without enumerating all cycles. Specifically, the method draws uniform spanning trees and collects the fundamental cycles created by their non-tree edges, such that each tree provides an informative subset of simple cycles. Because cycles are included with unequal probabilities and are dependent within each subset, we formulate an inclusion-probability-based Horvitz-Thompson estimator, which we average over random subsets, a procedure we call Monte Carlo Horvitz-Thompson. For this, we sample multiple Horvitz-Thompson estimators and introduce a method to further subsample the individual estimators for increased computational performance. For sampling cycles, the estimator is unbiased if exact cycle inclusion probabilities are known. To extend the method to larger networks, we derive an efficient mean-field approximation for the inclusion probabilities and characterize the graph regimes in which it remains accurate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world networks demonstrate the computational scaling and statistical performance of the framework. We then illustrate the utility of Monte Carlo Horvitz-Thompson estimation by estimating cycle counts and cycle-level frustration statistics in signed spin systems. An implementation is available in the py-raccoon package.

entry.title: Joint Modeling of Conditional Mean and Variability in Multilevel Functional Data: Application to Postprandial Glucose Trajectories in the AEGIS Study

link.title: Joint Modeling of Conditional Mean and Variability in Multilevel Functional Data: Application to Postprandial Glucose Trajectories in the AEGIS Study

entry.content: Functional data analysis provides a framework for studying time-varying associations between covariates and high-frequency biological signals. In digital health, participants often contribute repeated functional trajectories, yet existing multilevel regression methods largely focus on the conditional mean, overlooking variability and its role in biological heterogeneity. We propose a heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects regression framework that jointly models the conditional mean and variance of repeated trajectories, with participant-specific random effects in both components. We also develop a participant-level bootstrap to quantify uncertainty in estimated functional parameters. We apply the method to postprandial glucose trajectories from the AEGIS study. Premeal glucose, carbohydrate intake, and meal type show distinct time-dependent associations with glucose variability, whereas HbA1c is more strongly associated with the conditional mean than with variability. Substantial between-participant differences in residual variability remain even after accounting for observed covariates. These findings show that modeling conditional variability alongside the mean provides insights into glucose regulation and individual heterogeneity that mean-focused analyses may miss. More broadly, the proposed framework enables joint characterization of average responses, variability, and participant-specific heterogeneity in repeated biological signals.

entry.title: Intensity-Based Estimation of Extreme Value Models for Highly Censored Data via a Latent Poisson Process

link.title: Intensity-Based Estimation of Extreme Value Models for Highly Censored Data via a Latent Poisson Process

entry.content: Extreme value theory provides a natural framework for modelling rare events and extrapolating tail probabilities, but its direct application to survival analysis is complicated by right censoring, heterogeneous follow-up, and the need for coherent inference beyond the range of the observed data. We propose a Bayesian survival model that integrates extreme value theory with a hazard-based formulation built upon the extended generalized Pareto distribution. Rather than separating the bulk and tail of the distribution through an explicit threshold, the proposed model represents the entire hazard function within a unified parametric framework, allowing moderate and extreme survival times to be analysed simultaneously while preserving the asymptotic tail behaviour implied by extreme value theory. Inference is performed through a two-stage procedure. We further develop bias-correction procedures based on latent representative locations and adaptive partition refinement, and establish theoretical results showing the asymptotic consistency of the proposed approximation under standard regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate that the methodology provides reliable uncertainty quantification across a wide range of tail regimes, censoring proportions, and sample sizes, while remaining robust under moderate model misspecification. The practical performance of the approach is illustrated through an analysis of a heart failure cohort, where the proposed model enables inference on long-term survival probabilities and tail behaviour beyond the observed follow-up period. The resulting framework offers a computationally feasible and theoretically grounded alternative for modelling censored survival data when inference on extreme survival times is of primary scientific interest.

entry.title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks

link.title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks

entry.content: We propose a doubly-robust method to estimate the causal effects of multi-valued treatment regimes on patient outcomes. A multi-valued treatment regime assigns personalized treatments from a set of competing options based on a patient’s history. Existing methods for optimal treatment regimes are largely limited to binary or continuous treatments. We extend the longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimator (LTMLE) to accommodate multi-valued treatments by modeling treatment assignments with a multinomial model. We further integrate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) into the LTMLE framework as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models, and compare this approach to ensemble machine learning. Simulation studies show that LTMLE with either ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased, with close to nominal coverage, whereas sequential g-computation with ensemble machine learning is substantially biased under a dynamic rule. A multinomial treatment model performs similarly to a series of binomial regressions with ensemble machine learning, but yields more stable inference when the treatment model is an RNN.

entry.title: Between Hi-Fi and MMI: the overlap of redundancy and synergy in partial information decomposition

link.title: Between Hi-Fi and MMI: the overlap of redundancy and synergy in partial information decomposition

entry.content: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that two sources carry about a target into redundant, unique and synergistic parts, with nonnegative decompositions lying on a segment where redundancy measures are bounded by the positive part of the co-information and the smaller source-target information. We parameterize this segment by the overlap, the common excess of redundancy and synergy over their net balance, and show that for many of the named PID measures, their redundancy can be written as the largest positive part of the co-information over a set of reference distributions. This common form induces an ordering of those PIDs on the segment. With the smallest redundancy and synergy and the largest unique atoms of any nonnegative PID, the information-theoretic version of Hi-Fi, a feature-importance method, is the zero-overlap end of the segment for two sources, with the maximum overlap bound given by the minimum mutual information (MMI) PID. We introduce, by splitting the co-information into a pairwise maximum- entropy part and the third-order connected information, a PID that sits at zero overlap except when pairwise redundancy and triadic synergy coexist. For three or more sources the bivariate results hold on every pair of merged source groups, and among all nonnegative solutions of the lattice equations MMI and Hi-Fi still give the smallest and largest unique atoms but zero overlap on all pairs at once is often unattainable. Two inequalities across pairs are necessary in general and sufficient for three sources. For identity targets zero overlap is possible exactly when the sources’ information diagram is nonnegative. In random three- and four-source distributions zero overlap on all pairs fails in 21-100% of the cases.

entry.title: Bounded GARCH Processes

link.title: Bounded GARCH Processes

entry.content: We propose a novel class of Bounded GARCH (B-GARCH) processes designed to characterise the conditional heteroskedasticity of continuous time series constrained within a compact interval. While standard GARCH specifications are tailored for R-valued data, many empirical series, such as realised correlation, unemployment rates, expenditure shares, and relative humidity, are bounded. Fitting a traditional GARCH model to such data creates a severe support mismatch, frequently generating predictions and density forecasts that breach the natural boundaries of the data (boundary violation). Furthermore, conventional approaches utilising non-linear link transformations onto the real line might induce interpretability issues and estimation biases. To address these limitations, our proposed B-GARCH framework ensures a proper predictive distribution and an equation for the dynamic conditional variance with a parameter constraint that strictly preserves the bounded support of the entire process almost surely. We establish the fundamental probabilistic properties of the process, proving strict stationarity and ergodicity, and address parameter estimation via conditional maximum likelihood. The asymptotic consistency and normality of the estimators are rigorously derived, and their finite-sample performance is validated through Monte Carlo simulations. An empirical application to the monthly realised correlation between the Vanguard Real Estate ETF (VNQ) and the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) demonstrates that B-GARCH models effectively capture volatility clustering while completely eliminating boundary violation issue that plagues traditional GARCH models.

entry.title: Fast Functional Clustering via Closed-Form Covariance Updates

link.title: Fast Functional Clustering via Closed-Form Covariance Updates

entry.content: Functional clustering identifies coordinated molecular profiles, but repeated numerical covariance optimization can make mixture-model fitting computationally demanding. We develop a fast functional clustering procedure for joint analysis across conditions, combining linear mean profiles on a standardized log niche coordinate with first-order structured antedependence (SAD(1)) covariance. Weighted residual statistics yield closed-form conditional covariance updates under four parameter-sharing specifications, while an innovation representation simplifies likelihood evaluation. In same-R comparisons with numerical optimization of identical conditional objectives, the closed-form solver was 91.5–201.4 times as fast, with objective agreement in all 60 targets. Under matched complete mixture fits, it achieved a 1.87–2.37-fold speedup with identical cluster assignments. Recovery simulations showed higher module classification accuracy and lower mean-curve error than $K$-means and a Gaussian mixture with shared full covariance when the mean structure was correctly specified. SAD(1) provided an additional recovery gain under strong residual correlation, whereas curved-mean controls identified the importance of an appropriate mean family. Applications to single-condition gut microbiota, paired leaf–root microbiota and three-visit human gut multi-omics illustrate the framework across different numbers of conditions. Closed-form covariance estimation makes joint functional clustering substantially faster while retaining the fitted model’s likelihood and assignments.
